This is Dave, answering emails at his desk at a perfectly normal speed.
Then he hears footsteps. His boss is walking past.
For eleven seconds, Dave is the hardest-working man in the building.
He sits up, types faster, and opens a spreadsheet he doesn't need.
Footsteps fade. Spreadsheet closes. Normal speed.
Psychologists have a name for Dave's eleven seconds. They call it the Hawthorne effect.
But does being watched really change what we do?
And if it does, which Dave is the real one?
The answer starts in a giant factory near Chicago, a hundred years ago,
with a light bulb committee, five women, a paper tape, and some missing data.
So let's start where they started, with the light.
In the nineteen twenties, Western Electric's Hawthorne Works made the phones and switches for the Bell telephone system.
It was so big it had its own hospital, its own fire brigade and its own greenhouse.
By nineteen twenty-nine, more than forty thousand people worked there.
In nineteen twenty-four, the factory agreed to help answer one question.
Does better lighting make workers faster?
The electric lighting industry was very interested,
and the committee behind the study had Thomas Edison as its honorary chairman.
They were hoping for a nice, simple result.
More light, more work, and more light bulbs.
So the engineers turned the lights up, and output mostly rose. The line went up.
Then they did it properly, with a second group whose lights stayed the same.
That group's line went up too.
So they turned the test group's lights down, step by step, and both lines kept going up.
Output only fell at the very bottom, when the women said they could hardly see what they were doing.
Then two volunteers were moved into a locker room,
with the light turned down to about the level of moonlight.
They kept working at the same speed.
They said their eyes felt fine, and they were less tired than under bright lights.
Which is not what a light bulb committee wants to hear.
And then came the strangest test of all. After days of brighter and brighter light,
the women watched an electrician swap the bulbs, for bulbs of exactly the same size.
The women said they liked the brighter light.
Their output, at every stage, barely changed.
The company decided that light was only one factor, and apparently a minor one.
No final report was ever written.
One historian suspects the answer just wasn't the one the industry wanted: buy more light bulbs.
But if it wasn't the light,
something was still making the line go up.
In April nineteen twenty-seven, the company tried again, with more control.
Five women who built telephone relays got a small room of their own.
A relay was about thirty-five tiny parts and four screws.
Each woman built one roughly every minute, about five hundred a day.
Every finished relay dropped down a chute
and punched one hole in a moving paper tape.
One hole, one relay, on the record forever.
And an observer sat with them, writing down everything they did and said.
Over the next two years, the company kept changing things.
Rest breaks. Shorter days. Saturday mornings off.
And a company sandwich at half past nine. Occasionally, tongue.
Breaks added, the line went up. Shorter days, the line went up.
In nineteen twenty-eight, the company asked a Harvard Business School professor, Elton Mayo, to help explain it.
That autumn, they took it all away.
Back to forty-eight hours a week, with no breaks and no sandwich.
If the breaks were the secret, output should have crashed.
Their speed per hour dipped a little.
But their weekly total hit a new record anyway.
Something in that room was making them work harder,
and it clearly wasn't the tongue.
Here's a clue. That autumn, at a little party after a medical check-up, the women chatted with the observer.
Say, he's no boss. We don't have any boss.
When the observer started to reply, another one of them told him to shut up.
Mayo's answer became famous. It wasn't the breaks, the hours or the food.
The women had become a team,
and the man watching them felt less like a boss and more like a friend.
Somebody was paying attention, and they responded. That's the version in the textbooks.
But there was one more change in that room,
one that almost nobody mentions. We'll come back to it.
In the nineteen fifties, the idea got a name,
and sociologist Henry Landsberger helped make it famous.
The Hawthorne effect. Watch people, and the line goes up.
Management books loved it. One bestseller noted that the best companies seemed to manage by creating an endless stream of Hawthorne effects.
And it shows up far from factories.
In two thousand fourteen, a Canadian hospital logged every squirt of hand gel and soap in two wards for eight months,
and tracked the auditors who walk the halls checking hand washing.
When an auditor was in sight, hallway hand washing roughly tripled.
And you don't even need a real person.
In two thousand six, psychologist Melissa Bateson's team at Newcastle University ran a test in their own coffee room.
Tea and coffee worked on trust.
You took a drink, and you dropped the money into an honesty box.
Above the price list, they put a picture that changed every week for ten weeks.
Either some flowers, or a pair of eyes.
In the weeks with eyes, people paid two point seven six times as much, for the same amount of milk.
Nobody was watching them. The eyes were printed on paper.
A department full of psychologists, paying extra because a printout was looking at them.
Dave printed a pair of eyes and taped them to his monitor.
He has never worked harder. He has also never felt so judged.
So that settles it, right? Watch people, even with paper, and the line goes up.
Well, not quite. For decades, the light experiment's data were believed to be destroyed.
In two thousand eleven, Chicago economists Steven Levitt and John List published the first real analysis,
from charts they'd found on old microfilm.
Every lighting change had been made on a Sunday, the one day the factory was closed.
And output jumped at the start of every week,
whether the lights had changed or not.
The famous pattern wasn't the light. It was the day off.
The remarkable patterns in the textbooks, they wrote, were entirely fictional.
They did find hints of something real, just much smaller.
And the relay room? Remember the change that almost nobody mentions? It was their pay.
In the main department, their earnings depended on a group of about a hundred.
In the test room, a group of five. Every extra relay now showed up in their pay.
Two women who chatted a lot and fell behind were swapped out.
And once, they slowed down on purpose, to get their breaks back.
They knew they were being watched, and they used it.
So is the Hawthorne effect just a myth?
In two thousand fourteen, Jim McCambridge's team reviewed nineteen studies built to test it.
Most found something, but it varied so much that there's no single Hawthorne effect.
And that hospital had one more detail. Inside the patient rooms, nothing changed.
The effect stayed in the hallway.
Even the paper eyes have wobbled. In lab games, they barely make people more generous,
though they may still cut littering.
Being watched does change us, but not like the legend, and not everywhere.
It changes what we do in the hallway,
wherever we think someone can see.
In nineteen seventy-six, test room worker Theresa Layman Zajac looked back.
I had no idea there would be so much happening and so many people watching us.
The tape counted every relay they made.
And one of them remembered what it didn't count.
We've been the best friends since the day we were in the test room.
Tomorrow, the footsteps will come, and Dave will sit up straight. Everyone has a hallway.
But footsteps fade. Who you are when nobody's watching
is whatever happens after they do.
Tonight, Dave is the last one in the office. No boss, no footsteps, no paper eyes.
He finishes the email he's been avoiding all week, and nobody will ever know.
His line goes up a little, and nobody's counting.
That's the part that counts.
